intro: The stance this platform takes is not a theory — it has been tried, in places large and small, for centuries and for decades. These are the cases we learn from: what happened, what the evidence shows, what each one teaches a county of 21,000 — including the case where direct democracy struggles, because a stance that hides its counterexamples isn't a stance, it's a pitch.

cases.title: The New England town meeting
cases.what_happened: For nearly four centuries, hundreds of New England towns have governed themselves by open meeting: any resident may attend, speak, and vote directly on budgets, bylaws, and local decisions. It is one of only three documented institutions of direct citizen assembly in world history, alongside the ancient Athenian ecclesia and the Swiss Landsgemeinde.
cases.what_evidence_shows: Durability. Town meetings survived the printing press, the telegraph, and the internet. Visiting in 1831, Alexis de Tocqueville wrote that New England town governments showed greater political independence than any municipal body he knew in Europe — he called town institutions the schools where liberty is learned.
cases.what_it_teaches: Direct local self-government is not an innovation to be piloted; it is a heritage to be extended. Clark County's quorum court with its public comment period is a descendant of this line. The platform's job is to widen the room — so the meeting includes people who can't be there at 6 p.m. on a second Monday.
cases.caveats: Attendance in modern town meetings has declined with town size — the same scale limit Switzerland shows. Direct assembly works best small, which is precisely the county scale.

cases.title: Switzerland — voting as a habit
cases.what_happened: Swiss citizens vote on roughly 15 substantive questions a year, at every level of government. More than a third of all national referendums ever held on Earth took place in Switzerland. In thousands of small communes, citizens still assemble to pass budgets directly.
cases.what_evidence_shows: Direct participation can be a routine of civic life rather than a crisis instrument. Research on Swiss municipalities finds assembly attendance and turnout are strongest in smaller communes and decline as municipal size grows — direct democracy's natural habitat is exactly county-sized.
cases.what_it_teaches: Frequency normalizes participation. One question at a time, asked plainly, on a predictable rhythm — the platform's issue lifecycle borrows the Swiss cadence at a scale where the evidence says it works best.
cases.caveats: Swiss referendums are binding, which requires constitutional machinery a county cannot and should not improvise. That is one reason this platform's results are signal, not command.

cases.title: vTaiwan — finding the hidden majority
cases.what_happened: Taiwan's government adopted an open process where citizens respond to statements — agree, disagree, pass — but can never reply to each other. Clustering software maps the opinion groups and surfaces statements that win support across them. The process reached 200,000 participants and produced real regulation: ride-sharing rules, online alcohol sales, revenge-porn law.
cases.what_evidence_shows: Under loud public fights, silent majorities repeatedly agreed on substantial common ground — and the no-replies mechanic is what let it surface. Participants competed to write statements that could win broad support instead of competing to dunk.
cases.what_it_teaches: Comment sections amplify fights because replies reward them. The platform inherits vTaiwan's core mechanics: statements without replies, agreement mapped across groups, bridge-building scored above winning. Deliberation mode (M7) is this, at county scale.
cases.caveats: vTaiwan worked because the government pre-committed to act on results. Our version starts without that commitment — which is why the launch issues are pre-agreed with officials who already want the answer.

cases.title: Porto Alegre — where residents moved the money
cases.what_happened: The city that invented participatory budgeting let neighborhood assemblies rank capital spending priorities. Tens of thousands of residents — disproportionately poor residents — decided real allocations year after year.
cases.what_evidence_shows: Roads, water connections, and school access measurably improved in underserved districts; government responsiveness and civic organization strengthened; residents who participated became more politically active afterward. Then the hard lesson: when political commitment faded in the 2000s, the gains eroded.
cases.what_it_teaches: Both halves. Participation moves real money toward real needs — and processes that depend on a champion die with the champion. That erosion is why this platform is built as durable public infrastructure: open source, config-driven, cheap enough to survive indifference, with a succession plan written before it's needed.
cases.caveats: Porto Alegre allocated binding budget shares; a county platform produces signal. The mechanism differs; the participation effects are what transfer.

cases.title: Better Reykjavik — half a city, one website
cases.what_happened: An open idea-and-debate platform where residents propose and argue for city improvements — with arguments for and against listed separately, never threaded. The city council committed to review the top ideas every month and publicly answer whether each was approved.
cases.what_evidence_shows: Over 70,000 participants out of 120,000 residents — better than 50% penetration, extraordinary for civic tech — with 30,000 registered users submitting 10,000 ideas. The monthly council-review commitment is widely credited as the engine: people participate when someone demonstrably reads the results.
cases.what_it_teaches: The loop is the product. Reykjavik's monthly council review is exactly the platform's outcome-page-and-packet design: every question ends with what the body actually did. Participation follows proof that participation lands.
cases.caveats: Iceland's civic culture and small scale helped; penetration like that takes years, not launches.

cases.title: Decidim — infrastructure that spread
cases.place: Barcelona, Spain — then hundreds of institutions
cases.what_happened: Barcelona built an open-source participation platform — proposals, budgets, assemblies, consultations — and released the software publicly. 25,000 residents signed up in its first two months and submitted over 10,000 proposals shaping the city's action plan.
cases.what_evidence_shows: Open-source civic infrastructure generalizes: Decidim now runs hundreds of instances across Europe, from small towns to regional governments, each with its own configuration on the same kernel.
cases.what_it_teaches: Build the kernel once, isolate the local specifics in configuration, give it away — a second county should be a config file and a folder of PDFs. That is this platform's architecture, chosen for the same reason Barcelona chose it.
cases.caveats: Big-city budgets built Decidim. The county version has to prove the same pattern survives on a dry cleaner's sponsorship — which is rather the point.

cases.title: Deliberative polling — what happens to people who participate
cases.what_happened: James Fishkin's method: gather a random sample, give them balanced briefing materials and moderated small-group discussion, measure opinions before and after. It has run over a hundred times across dozens of countries.
cases.what_evidence_shows: Participants gain measurable knowledge, and — the striking finding — a single deliberative weekend produced large effects on civic engagement and voting nearly a year later. Participants came to follow politics more closely and to see their own opinions as worth having. Honest note: shifts in specific policy views often faded with time; the engagement effects are what lasted.
cases.what_it_teaches: The deepest return on participation isn't any single result — it's what taking part does to the participant. A resident who answers one county question, sees the count, and watches the outcome close is measurably more likely to show up again, everywhere. The platform is an engagement engine wearing a budget site's clothes.
cases.caveats: Deliberative polls use random samples and paid weekends; a self-selected county platform must be honest that its participants choose themselves — which is what the representativeness display is for.

cases.title: Lahti — voting at the library
cases.what_happened: City-wide participatory budgeting where residents proposed ideas and voted on allocations — and, critically, anyone could vote in person at the public libraries, not just online.
cases.what_evidence_shows: Library voting materially changed who participated — reaching residents online-only processes never touch. The pilot succeeded well enough that the participatory budget doubled the following year.
cases.what_it_teaches: Hybrid isn't an accessibility gesture; it is what makes results representative enough to cite. Paper ballots at the library, the senior center, and the dry cleaner's counter are this platform's Lahti move.
cases.caveats: Municipal funding sustained it; the county version rides on cheaper rails by necessity.

sources.label: People Powered: participatory budgeting and participation

cases.title: Washington County, Wisconsin — a small county moves real money
cases.what_happened: County Executive Josh Schoemann led a priority-based budgeting process that reallocated 15% of the county's entire operating budget according to articulated priorities.
cases.what_evidence_shows: County-scale government — the same institutional form as Clark County — can restructure real money when priorities are made explicit and visible. Not a metropolis, not a pilot ward: a county.
cases.what_it_teaches: The quorum court is not too small to act on demonstrated priorities; small is where it's most possible. The missing ingredient is usually not authority but visible, credible priority signal — which is the product this platform ships.
cases.caveats: Led from the executive's office. The Clark version starts outside the courthouse, which is slower and sturdier.

cases.title: UK Parliament petitions — traction that guarantees an answer
cases.what_happened: Parliament's petition site lets any citizen post a question-shaped demand. The mechanic that made it matter: at 10,000 signatures the government is obligated to publish a response; at 100,000 the Petitions Committee considers it for a parliamentary debate — and usually holds one.
cases.what_evidence_shows: Millions participate because traction is convertible: a number of signatures becomes a guaranteed institutional act. The thresholds turn diffuse public feeling into a procedural event with a date and a record — even when the government's answer is no, the answer exists in public.
cases.what_it_teaches: A county platform cannot obligate officials — and doesn't need to. It can obligate itself: at 100 responses, the result is printed, hand-delivered to the relevant body, and the delivery stamped publicly. Receipt is guaranteed by us; the response becomes part of the official's public record either way. That is the traction rule on the open questions page.
cases.caveats: Westminster's thresholds bind because Parliament adopted them. Ours bind only the platform — which is honest, and also the only version that doesn't require permission to start.

cases.title: Tupelo, Mississippi — the poorest county becomes the marvel
cases.what_happened: In the 1940s, Lee County was among the poorest counties in the nation's poorest state. A local newspaper publisher, George McLean, organized what became the Tupelo model: seventeen businessmen staked a dairy program, the Community Development Foundation formed in 1948 to recruit industry, and — the distinctive move — rural community development councils brought farm families and townspeople into the same rooms to solve shared problems, decade after decade.
cases.what_evidence_shows: Lee County rose from the state's poorest ranks to among its most affluent, building traditions of interracial cooperation and civic giving that community development scholars still study as 'the Tupelo miracle.' The engine wasn't a factory or a windfall — it was organized, patient, local cooperation with a newspaper holding the record.
cases.what_it_teaches: The closest analog to Clark County in the whole library: a small rural Southern county with no natural advantages that changed its trajectory through organized community structures and a local institution keeping score in public. The platform's docket, questions, and open records are digital rural community development councils — the same rooms, wider doors.
cases.caveats: Tupelo's rise took forty years and a generation of sustained local leadership; no case in this library was fast.

cases.title: Chattanooga — from dirtiest city to National Park City, starting with 1,700 residents
cases.what_happened: In 1969 the federal government named Chattanooga the worst city in America for particulate air pollution — nylon stockings reportedly disintegrated outdoors. The city passed its air ordinance within months and reached full industrial compliance by 1972. Then in 1984 came the deeper turn: Vision 2000, a community visioning process where about 1,700 residents proposed and voted on 2,500 ideas, distilled to 40 public goals.
cases.what_evidence_shows: By 1992, Vision 2000 had produced 223 implemented programs and projects — the Tennessee Aquarium and riverfront revival most famously. Four decades on, the once-dirtiest city is North America's first National Park City, with a municipal fiber network and an outdoor economy. The trajectory change is traceable to a participatory process: residents at large, not a hand-picked committee, set the goals.
cases.what_it_teaches: Mass participation isn't the celebration after a turnaround — in the best-documented American case, it was the ignition. A county that can ask its residents structured questions and publish honest counts owns the same ignition system Chattanooga used, at county scale, standing.
cases.caveats: Chattanooga had foundation money (Lyndhurst) and a metro's scale; the mechanism transfers, the budget doesn't.

cases.title: The Promise towns — Kalamazoo, El Dorado, and Arkadelphia itself
cases.place: Kalamazoo, MI · El Dorado, AR · Arkadelphia, AR
cases.what_happened: In 2005 anonymous donors promised every Kalamazoo public school graduate free in-state college tuition. Murphy Oil brought the model to El Dorado, Arkansas in 2007. And in 2010 the Ross Foundation and Southern Bancorp brought it home: the Arkadelphia Promise has awarded more than $1.17 million to Arkadelphia High graduates.
cases.what_evidence_shows: The Upjohn Institute's long-run research on Kalamazoo: four-year college enrollment up 34%, credential completion up from 36% to 48% of eligible graduates, low-income completion up more than 50%, and district enrollment grew 26% while peer districts shrank — a scholarship that changed a town's population curve. El Dorado's eligible graduates' college attendance rose from about 60% to over 80%. And Arkadelphia's own numbers: the Class of 2011 was the first Promise class; within four graduating classes the program had funded 718 college semesters; 44% of recipients start at Henderson State and 14% at Ouachita Baptist — the scholarship money circulates back through the town's own universities; and the first class's freshman-to-sophomore retention hit 70%, beating the Arkansas average of 61.4%.
cases.what_it_teaches: Trajectory change can be bought deliberately, locally, and per-child — and Clark County already owns a working piece of the toolkit. The platform's job here is the same as everywhere: make the investment and its results navigable, so the county can see what its Promise produces and decide, together, what to build next to it.
cases.caveats: Promise programs need durable funders — El Dorado's outlived Murphy Oil's headquarters, but the dependence is real. And scholarships lift trajectories over decades, not budget cycles.

cases.title: California's propositions — the cautionary case
cases.what_happened: California's binding statewide initiative system lets anyone with enough signatures put law directly on the ballot. It has produced landmark policy and persistent pathologies: a paid-signature industry, one-sided drafting without compromise, voter fatigue across dozens of complex measures, and campaigns where money buys reach.
cases.what_evidence_shows: The criticisms are real: initiative drafting doesn't incorporate the compromise that legislative debate forces, and measures like Proposition 8 showed majorities can vote directly against a minority's rights. The research record is more mixed than the caricature — studies find voter competence fears overstated, and mass electorates are actually harder for special interests to lobby than legislators are — but the failure modes are documented and serious.
cases.what_it_teaches: Every design choice in this platform is an answer to a California failure mode. Binding statewide law → non-binding county signal, officials retain authority and legal responsibility. Paid signatures → no signature threshold to buy; a neutrality pipeline instead. One-sided drafting → the wording review and the offered neutral rewrite. Ballot fatigue → few questions, open one at a time, each with a cited context page. Majority-against-minority → bright lines in the charter: no candidates, no ballot measures, no named individuals, and questions about process rather than groups. The cautionary case isn't an argument against asking residents — it's the specification for asking them carefully.
cases.caveats: Honesty requires the converse too: California's system, for all its flaws, has repeatedly forced issues legislators preferred to bury. The lesson is design, not abstinence.
